lessons.title: Introduction to Blacksmithing: Forge Setup and Safety
lessons.body:
Blacksmithing is the art of shaping metal using heat and hammer. In Africa, traditional blacksmiths have worked iron for centuries, and today you can set up a simple forge using locally available materials. A basic forge needs a heat source, an air supply, and a fireproof hearth. You can build a forge from a car brake drum, a metal bucket lined with clay, or even a hole in the ground lined with mud. The fire should be fueled with charcoal, which is widely available. For air, use a hand-cranked blower, a hair dryer, or a bellows made from leather and wood. The air pipe (tuyere) should enter the fire from the side, about 10 cm above the bottom.

Safety is critical. Always wear leather gloves, safety glasses, and a leather apron. Never wear synthetic clothingâit melts. Work in a well-ventilated area, as forging produces carbon monoxide. Keep a bucket of water and a fire extinguisher nearby. The metal must be heated to 800â1200Â°C, which is bright orange to yellow. At this temperature, it becomes soft like clay. Use tongs to hold the metalânever your hands. Quench hot metal in water or oil to cool it. Remember that hot metal looks the same as cold metal; always test with a magnet or water drop before touching.

Start your fire with small pieces of charcoal, then add more as it catches. Use the blower to get a steady, hot fire. The ideal forge fire is a deep bed of coals with a bright center. Place your metal in the hottest part, called the 'sweet spot'. Heat it until it's the right color, then move quickly to the anvil. Work efficiently because the metal cools fast. A good forge setup is the foundation of all blacksmithing, so take time to build it right.

lessons.title: Basic Forging Techniques: Drawing Out, Upsetting, Bending
lessons.body:
Drawing out means making metal longer and thinner. Heat your metal to bright orange (around 1000Â°C). Place it on the anvil and strike with the hammer's flat face. Hit at a slight angle, moving the metal away from you. Turn the metal 90 degrees after each blow to keep it square. Use the horn of the anvil for curves. For a 1 cm square bar, you can draw it out to 6 mm thick in about 10 heats. Work from the center outward to avoid creating cold shuts (folds).

Upsetting is the opposite: making metal shorter and thicker. Heat a section of your bar, then strike the end against the anvil or a solid block. This forces the metal to bulge. For a decorative knob, heat the last 5 cm to yellow, hold it vertically, and hammer the end down. Upsetting is useful for making rivet heads or thickening edges. Be careful not to overheatâif it sparks, it's burning.

Bending is simple but must be done at forging temperature. Use the anvil's horn or a bending fork. For a sharp bend, place the metal over the edge of the anvil and strike near the bend. For a smooth curve, use the horn. You can also bend cold metal in a vise, but it may crack. Always bend with the grain if possible. Practice these three techniques on scrap metal. A good blacksmith can draw out, upset, and bend with precision. In Africa, these skills are used to make tools, art, and household items. Remember: heat, hammer, and control.

lessons.title: Using Anvils, Hammers, and Tongs
lessons.body:
The anvil is your main work surface. A good anvil is made of hardened steel and weighs 50â150 kg. In Africa, you can find used anvils at scrap yards or make one from a piece of railway track. Mount it at knuckle height on a sturdy stump. The flat face is for general hammering. The horn is for bending and shaping curves. The hardy hole holds tools like cutters, and the pritchel hole is for punching. Keep the anvil clean and free of scale. Never hammer on the anvil's face with a hardened hammerâit can chip.

Hammers come in various weights. For general forging, use a 1â2 kg cross-peen or ball-peen hammer. The cross-peen is for drawing out, and the ball-peen for texturing. Hold the hammer near the end of the handle for power, or near the head for control. Strike with a relaxed grip, letting the hammer's weight do the work. Don't grip too tightâit causes fatigue. For heavy work, use a sledgehammer with a striker. Always wear safety glasses.

Tongs are essential for holding hot metal. You need several types: flat-jaw for square bars, bolt-jaw for round stock, and pick-up tongs for small pieces. Make your own tongs from mild steel by forging the jaws to fit your work. Adjust them by heating and bending. Never use pliersâthey slip. When holding hot metal, keep the tongs parallel to the anvil. Your hammer hand should be free. Practice picking up and moving hot metal until it's second nature. Good tools make good work.

lessons.title: Heat Treating and Annealing Metal
lessons.body:
Heat treating changes the hardness and toughness of steel. Annealing softens metal so you can work it. To anneal, heat the metal to non-magnetic (around 800Â°C for high-carbon steel), then bury it in dry ash, sand, or vermiculite. Let it cool slowly overnight. This relieves stress and makes filing and drilling easier. In Africa, wood ash from a fire works well.

Hardening makes steel tough. Heat the metal to critical temperature (bright orange, non-magnetic), then quench it quickly in water, oil, or brine. Water cools fastest, oil slower. For most tools, use oil (motor oil or vegetable oil). Quench vertically to avoid warping. The metal becomes hard but brittle. Test with a fileâit should skate without cutting.

Tempering reduces brittleness. After hardening, clean the metal and heat it gently until it turns a specific color. For a chisel, heat until it's straw yellow (220Â°C); for a spring, blue (300Â°C). Then quench again. This gives a tough, usable tool. Practice on scrap steel. Different steels require different temperatures. If you don't know the steel type, experiment. Heat treating is the difference between a tool that lasts and one that breaks. Always wear gloves and eye protection.

lessons.title: Twisting and Texturing Metal
lessons.body:
Twisting adds decorative flair to metal. Heat a square bar to bright orange. Clamp one end in a vise and use a wrench or tongs to twist the other end. For a uniform twist, turn slowly and keep the heat even. A 1 cm bar can be twisted 2â3 full turns over 20 cm. If it cools, reheat. You can twist multiple bars together for a rope effect. In Africa, twisted iron is used in furniture, gates, and art. Practice on 6 mm square stock.

Texturing creates surface patterns. Use a hammer with a rounded face or a chisel to make marks. The ball-peen hammer gives dimples. A cross-peen makes lines. You can also use a punch to make dots. For a hammered look, strike the metal repeatedly with a ball-peen while it's at low orange heat. Work on a sandbag or wood to avoid flattening. Another method is to use a spring fuller or a guillotine tool to make grooves. Always work on a clean anvil.

For a rustic look, brush the hot metal with a wire brush to remove scale, then apply wax or oil while warm. This gives a black finish. You can also use a brass brush to add color. Texturing is about experimentation. Try different hammers and techniques. Remember to anneal if the metal gets too hard. These decorative techniques turn simple forgings into art.

lessons.title: Project: Forged Abstract Form
lessons.body:
Now you will create an abstract sculpture using the skills you've learned. This project combines drawing out, bending, twisting, and texturing. You will need a 1 m length of 10 mm mild steel round bar, a forge, anvil, hammer, tongs, and a wire brush. Start by drawing out one end to a taper. Heat the last 10 cm to orange and hammer it to a point. This will be a leg or spike.

Next, create a twist in the middle. Heat a 15 cm section and twist it 3 full turns. Then bend the bar into a flowing curve using the anvil's horn. Heat as needed. Add a second taper on the other end. Now, upset one section to make a thicker node. Heat a 5 cm section and hammer it against the anvil to thicken it. This creates visual weight. Use the ball-peen hammer to texture the surface with dimples. Work while the metal is at low orange.

Finally, decide on a base. You can weld the sculpture to a metal plate or set it in a concrete base. For a free-standing form, ensure it balances. Clean the finished piece with a wire brush, then apply beeswax or linseed oil while warm. This protects it from rust. Display your abstract form. Remember, abstract art is about expressionâthere are no mistakes, only variations. This project proves you can forge, shape, and finish metal. With these skills, you can create saleable art for local markets or commissions.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Forging and Shaping for African Metal Sculpture Studios

This practical reference supports the Forging and Shaping module of the Rise Africa Skills Metal Sculpture course. It is written for artisans, workshop owners, and apprentices who intend to turn metal sculpture into a reliable income stream â not just a creative hobby. Every technique here is chosen because it is repeatable, teachable, and compatible with the tools and materials most commonly available in African urban and peri-urban workshops: scrap vehicle springs, railway steel, rebar, mild steel plate, and charcoal or gas forges.

Blacksmithing and forging sit at the foundation of decorative and functional metalwork across the continent â from Ghanaian and Nigerian wrought-iron gate traditions to Senegalese and South African sculptural work sold to galleries and export buyers. The commercial logic is simple: forged work commands higher prices than welded assembly because it demonstrates skill, produces unique forms, and resists imitation. This reference consolidates setup, technique, tooling, heat treatment, surface work, and a project brief into one usable document.

1. Forge Setup and Safety in an African Workshop Context

Most successful sculpture workshops in Nairobi, Accra, Lagos, and Johannesburg start with a solid-fuel forge built from local materials: a car brake drum or wheel rim as the firepot, clay or firebrick lining, a steel pipe for the tuyere, and a hand-cranked or electric blower. Charcoal is widely available and cheaper than gas in many regions, though gas forges offer cleaner, faster heating for small work. Choose based on your electricity reliability and fuel logistics, not on prestige.

Site the forge with at least 3 metres of clear space, on a non-combustible floor, with cross-ventilation or an overhead hood. Keep quench water, a first-aid kit, and a dry-powder extinguisher within arm's reach. Good light matters for judging colour temperature â the single most important skill in forging.

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE LIGHTING THE FORGE
  • Carbon monoxide: never burn charcoal or coal in an enclosed room. CO is odourless and kills. Forge outdoors or under an open-sided shelter with a working flue.
  • Hot metal looks like cold metal: below roughly 550 Â°C, steel shows no glow. Always test with tongs, never with fingers.
  • Eye protection: wear impact-rated goggles or a face shield during forging and grinding. Chipping scale causes permanent eye injury.
  • Burns: keep a bucket of clean water and burn gel on site. Never quench a burn with forge water â it is contaminated.
  • Fuel storage: store charcoal, coal, and gas cylinders away from the forge, in a ventilated area, never near the fire.
  • Hearing: anvil work exceeds 100 dB. Use ear plugs during heavy striking sessions.

2. Basic Forging Techniques: Drawing Out, Upsetting, Bending

These three operations are the alphabet of forged sculpture. Master them and you can make almost any abstract or figurative form.

  • Drawing out â lengthening and thinning stock by striking with the hammer face at the anvil's horn or edge. Keep the work at a bright orange-yellow (roughly 950â1150 Â°C for mild steel). Rotate 90Â° between blows to avoid a "fish-mouth" end.
  • Upsetting â thickening or shortening by striking the end of the bar while it rests on the anvil face. It is the fastest way to build mass for a joint or a sculptural foot.
  • Bending â use the horn for curves, the edge for sharp angles, and a bending fork or scroll wrench for controlled radii. Bend while hot; cold bending cracks high-carbon scrap.

For sculpture, the commercial trick is consistency: a buyer of a series of ten forged bowls or abstract forms expects each to match. Practice the same operation on offcuts until the results are repeatable before you commit expensive stock.

3. Using Anvils, Hammers, and Tongs

An anvil is the single largest tool investment in a forging studio. A 50â80 kg London-pattern anvil, even a used one, is worth more than three cheap cast-iron substitutes because it rebounds the hammer and saves your arm. Mount it at knuckle height on a hardwood stump or a sand-filled steel drum â this also reduces noise complaints in dense urban workshops.

Hammers: start with a 1â1.5 kg cross-peen for drawing out, a 1 kg ball-peen for texturing, and a lighter 0.5 kg hammer for detail. Tongs must match the stock â flat-jaw for plate, bolt-jaw for square bar, and wolf-jaw for round. Make your own tongs from scrap spring steel; it is a core employability skill and a sellable product in itself.

4. Heat Treating and Annealing Metal

Heat treatment is where most African sculpture workshops lose money: pieces crack, warp, or fail to hold a finish. The rules below apply to the medium- and high-carbon steels commonly found in scrap vehicle springs, files, and bearings â the same stock used for forged blades, chisels, and decorative tooling.

Table 1. Heat treatment schedule for common scrap steels used in African forging workshops
Process Temperature Colour cue Cooling medium Purpose
Annealing ~800â850 Â°C Cherry red Cool slowly in ash or vermiculite Softens steel for filing, drilling, shaping
Normalising ~850â900 Â°C Bright cherry red Air cool Relieves internal stress after forging
Hardening ~780â830 Â°C Non-magnetic, cherry red Warm water or oil Hardens cutting edges and tooling
Tempering ~200â300 Â°C Straw to blue oxide Air cool Reduces brittleness, adds toughness

Source: temperatures and colour cues consolidated from ASM Handbook Volume 4: Heat Treating (ASM International) and the UK's Blacksmithing and Metalwork guidance published by the Worshipful Company of Blacksmiths.

For pure sculptural work in mild steel, heat treatment is usually unnecessary â but annealing is invaluable when you must drill, tap, or file a forged form. Always normalise a piece after heavy forging to prevent delayed cracking in storage or transit.

5. Twisting and Texturing Metal

Twisting and texturing add value at almost zero material cost. A plain bar becomes a sculptural element with 20 minutes of skilled work.

  • Twisting: heat a section evenly, clamp one end in a vice, and turn the other with a wrench or twisting fork. Count turns to keep a series consistent.
  • Texturing: use a ball-peen hammer, a cross-peen, a chisel, or a home-made stamp to create scale, bark, or fabric-like patterns. Work at a dull red to avoid cracking.
  • Surface finish: wire-brush hot, then apply beeswax, linseed oil, or a locally mixed patina. In humid coastal markets, a wax finish plus a clear lacquer extends outdoor life by years.

6. Costing and Pricing a Forged Piece

African buyers â local galleries, hotels, exporters, and diaspora customers â pay for story plus finish. A forged abstract form priced only on material and hours will lose money. Use a simple costed model, then apply a margin that reflects skill and market positioning.

Table 2. Indicative costing model for a 60 cm forged abstract sculpture (USD, workshop-level)
Cost line Typical range Notes
Steel stock (scrap, ~8 kg) $4 â $12 Vehicle spring, rebar, plate offcuts
Fuel (charcoal or LPG) $3 â $8 Rises sharply if forge is inefficient
Consumables (electrodes, grinding discs, wax, oil) $2 â $6 Often underestimated
Labour (8â14 hours at $2â$6/hr) $16 â $84 Reflects local market and skill level
Overheads (rent, tools depreciation, power) $4 â $12 Allocate per piece, not per month
Finishing, packing, transport $3 â $10 Crating for export adds more
Total cost $32 â $132 Before margin
Suggested wholesale price $80 â $300 2â2.5Ã cost for gallery/export
Suggested retail / direct-to-buyer $150 â $600 Higher for signed, exhibited work

Source: cost structure adapted from UNIDO's Small-scale Metalworking Enterprises technical reports and the African Development Bank's Creative Industries sector notes on artisan pricing.

7. Project: Forged Abstract Form

Brief: design and forge a freestanding abstract form, 40â80 cm tall, using at least three of the techniques above (drawing out, upsetting, bending, twisting, texturing). The piece must stand unsupported, have a stable base, and carry a consistent finish.

Suggested workflow:

  1. Sketch three ideas; choose the one you can forge in 10â14 hours.
  2. Cut stock to length; normalise scrap spring steel before shaping.
  3. Forge the base first â it controls stability.
  4. Build the main form, then add twisted or textured details.
  5. Weld or forge-weld joints; grind clean.
  6. Wire-brush hot, apply wax or oil finish.
  7. Photograph in natural light for your portfolio and online sales.

This project is deliberately commercial: it produces a photographable, shippable, repeatable product that can be sold as a one-off or as a small series. Document every step â buyers and grant panels reward evidence of process.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Forge outdoors or under a working flue â CO kills silently.
  • â Wear goggles, ear plugs, leather apron, and closed boots.
  • â Heat to bright orange-yellow before drawing out; never forge dull red.
  • â Rotate the bar 90Â° between hammer blows to keep sections square.
  • â Match tongs to stock shape â flat, bolt-jaw, or wolf-jaw.
  • â Normalise after heavy forging; anneal before drilling or filing.
  • â Count twists and blows so a series stays consistent.
  • â Cost every piece with material, fuel, labour, and overheads before quoting.

Further Reading (Free, Official Sources)

  • Smithsonian Institution â Blacksmithing: A Manual for Schools and Shops (public domain, free PDF)
  • Practical Action Publishing â free technical briefs on metalworking and small-scale forging
  • UNIDO â technical reports on small-scale metalworking enterprises
  • African Development Bank â creative industries and artisan sector notes
  • ASM International â public technical resources on heat treating (selected free content)

This reference is part of the Rise Africa Skills Metal Sculpture course and is intended for workshop use. Verify all temperatures and safety procedures against your local regulations and equipment before forging.

quiz.q: What is the ideal material for lining a simple forge?
quiz.explanation: Clay or mud is heat-resistant and widely available.

quiz.q: At what temperature does steel become soft enough to forge?
quiz.explanation: Steel is forged between 800Â°C and 1200Â°C, appearing bright orange to yellow.

quiz.q: Why should you never wear synthetic clothing in a forge?
options: B) It melts and sticks to skin
quiz.explanation: Synthetic fabrics melt when exposed to heat, causing severe burns.

quiz.q: What is the 'sweet spot' in a forge fire?
quiz.explanation: The sweet spot is the hottest part of the fire where metal heats fastest.

quiz.q: Which technique makes metal longer and thinner?
quiz.explanation: Drawing out stretches the metal, making it longer and thinner.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of turning metal 90 degrees after each hammer blow?
quiz.explanation: Turning the metal maintains a square cross-section and prevents flattening.

quiz.q: Upsetting is used to:
options: B) Make metal shorter and thicker
quiz.explanation: Upsetting compresses the metal, making it shorter and thicker.

quiz.q: What happens if you overheat metal during upsetting?
quiz.explanation: Overheating causes the metal to spark and burn, ruining it.

quiz.q: Which part of the anvil is used for bending curves?
quiz.explanation: The horn is rounded and used for bending and shaping curves.

quiz.q: What is the hardy hole on an anvil used for?
quiz.explanation: The hardy hole holds square-shanked tools like cutters or fullers.

quiz.q: What weight hammer is recommended for general forging?
quiz.explanation: A 1-2 kg hammer is suitable for most forging tasks.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using pliers to hold hot metal?
quiz.explanation: Pliers do not grip hot metal securely and can slip, causing injury.

quiz.q: Annealing is done to:
quiz.explanation: Annealing softens metal by slow cooling, making it easier to work.

quiz.q: What is the critical temperature for hardening steel?
quiz.explanation: Steel becomes non-magnetic at around 800Â°C, which is the critical temperature for hardening.

quiz.q: Which quenching medium cools fastest?
quiz.explanation: Water cools metal faster than oil or air, resulting in a harder but more brittle product.

quiz.q: Tempering is done to:
quiz.explanation: Tempering reduces brittleness after hardening, making the metal tough.

quiz.q: What color indicates the correct temper for a chisel?
quiz.explanation: Straw yellow (around 220Â°C) is the tempering color for chisels.

quiz.q: How many full turns can a 1 cm bar be twisted over 20 cm?
quiz.explanation: A 1 cm bar can typically be twisted 2-3 full turns over 20 cm for a uniform twist.

quiz.q: What tool is used to make dimples in metal?
quiz.explanation: The ball-peen hammer has a rounded face that creates dimples when struck.

quiz.q: Why should you work on a sandbag or wood when texturing?
options: A) To avoid flattening the metal
quiz.explanation: Working on a soft surface prevents the metal from flattening and preserves texture.

quiz.q: What finish can be applied to hot metal for a black look?
quiz.explanation: Applying wax or oil to hot metal creates a black protective finish.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the abstract form project?
quiz.explanation: The project begins by drawing out one end to a taper.

quiz.q: How long should the metal be for the abstract form project?
quiz.explanation: The project uses a 1 m length of 10 mm mild steel round bar.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of upsetting a section in the project?
quiz.explanation: Upsetting thickens a section, adding visual weight to the sculpture.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to clean scale from hot metal?
quiz.explanation: A wire brush removes scale and prepares the surface for finishing.

quiz.q: What is a good base for a free-standing forged sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Concrete or a metal plate provides a stable, durable base.

quiz.q: Why is it important to anneal metal before filing?
options: B) To soften it for easier cutting
quiz.explanation: Annealing softens the metal, making filing and drilling easier.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential for forging?
options: B) Leather gloves, apron, and safety glasses
quiz.explanation: Leather gloves, apron, and safety glasses protect against burns and flying debris.

quiz.q: What is the function of the tuyere in a forge?
options: B) To supply air to the fire
quiz.explanation: The tuyere is the air pipe that delivers air to the fire to increase heat.

quiz.q: What is the best way to test if metal is hot without touching it?
options: B) Use a magnet or water drop
quiz.explanation: A magnet or water drop can indicate temperature without risking burns.
